input: How does grappling work?
expected_behavior: Explains the grapple mechanic (contested Athletics vs Athletics/Acrobatics check, escape DC, speed drops to 0) using strictly the indexed Player's Handbook text. Must include at least one citation with tome name, section, and page matching grapple rules. Must not bleed mechanics from other systems.

To clarify how grappling works, let's break it down into its key components.

First, to initiate a grapple, you must make a grapple check, which is a Strength (Athletics) check contested by the target's Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check, depending on the target's size. The target must be within your reach and no more than one size larger than you.

If you succeed on the grapple check, you subject the target to the grappled condition, which reduces their speed to 0 and makes them unable to benefit from any bonus to their speed. The grapple ends when the grappler is incapacitated, the target is removed from the reach of the grappler or grappling effect, or when you release the target (no action required).

While the target is grappled, you can use your action to try to pin them, which requires another grapple check. If you succeed, you and the target are both restrained until the grapple ends.

It's worth noting that the Prerequisite: Strength 13ar higher feature allows you to gain additional benefits while grappling, such as advantage on attack rolls against a creature you are grappling and creatures that are one size larger than you don't automatically succeed on checks to escape your grapple. However, these benefits are optional and require the feature to be taken.

input: How does advantage and disadvantage work?
expected_behavior: Describes rolling two d20s and taking the higher/lower, and that multiple sources of advantage/disadvantage cancel out or do not stack. Grounded in retrieved excerpts with a correct citation.
actual_result:
Advantage and disadvantage in D&D 5e work as follows: when you have either advantage or disadvantage on an ability check, attack roll, or saving throw, you roll a second d20 in addition to the first roll. 

If you have advantage, you use the higher of the two rolls. If you have disadvantage, you use the lower roll. 

There are exceptions to this rule, however. If circumstances cause a roll to have both advantage and disadvantage, you are considered to have neither of them, and you roll only one d20. Additionally, if multiple circumstances affect a roll, you only roll one additional d20, even if some grant advantage and others impose disadvantage. 

Finally, if you have advantage or disadvantage and a special ability or spell grants you the ability to reroll one of the dice, you can do so, but only on one of the dice.

input: How does resting work?
expected_behavior: Explains short rest (1 hour, spend Hit Dice) and long rest (8 hours, regain HP and half Hit Dice) as stated in the Player's Handbook, with citations.
actual_result:
Resting in D&D 5e is a crucial aspect of a character's daily routine. According to the Player's Handbook, a character can take either a short rest or a long rest to recharge.

A short rest is a period of downtime that lasts at least 1 hour, during which a character can do light activities such as eating, drinking, reading, and tending to wounds. At the end of a short rest, a character can regain hit points equal to the total of one or more Hit Dice, with each Hit Die rolled and added to the character's Constitution modifier.

On the other hand, a long rest is a period of extended downtime that lasts at least 8 hours, during which a character sleeps or performs light activities. If the rest is interrupted by strenuous activity, the character must begin the rest again to gain any benefits from it. A character can't benefit from more than one long rest in a 24-hour period, and they must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

Additionally, resting is also important for spellcasters, as it allows them to restore their spell slots. According to the Spell Slots section, finishing a long rest restores any expended spell slots, while short rests do not have this effect.

In summary, resting in D&D 5e is a way for characters to recharge their hit points, regain spent Hit Dice, and restore their spell slots, depending on the type and duration of the rest.

A long rest is a period of extended downtime, at least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps or performs light activity: reading, talking, eating, or standing watch for no more than 2 hours. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity-at least 1hour of walking, fighting, casting spells, or similar adventuring activitythe characters must begin the rest again to gain any benefit from it.
A character can't benefit from more than one long rest in a 24-hour period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.
At the end of a long rest, a character regains alllost hit points. The character also regains spent Hit Dice, up to a number of dice equal to half of the character's total number of them. For example, if a character has eight Hit Dice, he or she can regain four spent Hit Dice upon finishing a long resto

A character can spend one or more Hit Dice at the end of a short rest, up to the character's maximum number of Hit Dice, which is equal to the character's leveI. For each Hit Die spent in this way, the player rolls the die and adds the character's Constitution modifier to it. The character regains hit points equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll. A character regains some spent Hit Dice upon finishing a long rest, as explained below.

Heroic though they might be, adventurers can't spend every hour of the day in the thick of exploration, social interaction, and combato They need rest-time to sleep and eat, tend their wounds, refresh their minds and spirits for spellcasting, and brace themselves for further adventure.
Adventurers can take short rests in the midst of an adventuring day and a long rest to end the day.

SPELL SLOTS
Regardless of how many spells a caster knows or prepares, he or she can cast only a limited number of spells before resting. Manipulating the fabric of magic and channeling its energy into even a simple spell is physically and mentally taxing, and higher-Ievel spells are even more so. input: Is the rule for cover the same as being hidden?

No, the rules for cover and hiding are not the same. 

According to the rules, a target has total cover if it is completely concealed by an obstacle (Section 197, COVER). In contrast, a target has half cover if an obstacle blocks at least half of its body (Section 197, COVER), and a target has three-quarters cover if about three-quarters of it is covered by an obstacle (Section 197, COVER). 

On the other hand, the Hide action (Section 193, HIDE) allows a character to make a Dexterity (Stealth) check to hide, and if successful, gain certain benefits. However, the Hide action does not provide cover, and the rules for cover are separate from the rules for hiding. 

In combat, a target with total cover cannot be targeted directly by an attack or a spell, but this is a specific rule related to area of effect attacks (Section 197, COVER). The Hide action, on the other hand, is a separate mechanic that allows a character to remain concealed, but it does not provide the same level of protection as cover.
